Let $x\in[l_x,u_x]$ and $y\in[l_y,u_y]$, where all four endpoints are finite and ordered, and let $w$ be an additional real variable representing the product $xy$. The **McCormick polytope** for this box is the set of $(x,y,w)$ satisfying the box bounds and
$$ w\ge l_xy+l_yx-l_xl_y,\qquad w\ge u_xy+u_yx-u_xu_y $$
$$ w\le u_xy+l_yx-u_xl_y,\qquad w\le l_xy+u_yx-l_xu_y $$
The term **McCormick envelope** will mean this polytope. Its exact relation to the convex hull of the product graph is established by the local bilinear-hull result.

A subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **convex** when, for all $x,y\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$ ([[def-interval]]), the point $(1-t)x+ty$ lies in $U$. Thus the full line segment from $x$ to $y$ remains in $U$.

derivations.claim: On the graph $w=xy$, subtracting the first lower plane from $xy$ gives $(x-l_x)(y-l_y)\ge0$, and subtracting the second lower plane gives $(u_x-x)(u_y-y)\ge0$. Subtracting $xy$ from the first upper plane gives $(u_x-x)(y-l_y)\ge0$, and subtracting it from the second upper plane gives $(x-l_x)(u_y-y)\ge0$. Thus every graph point satisfies all four inequalities.

If both widths are positive, put $s=u_x-l_x>0$, $t=u_y-l_y>0$, $X=(x-l_x)/s$, $Y=(y-l_y)/t$, and $W=(w-l_xy-l_yx+l_xl_y)/(st)$. The inequalities become $0\le X,Y\le1$, $W\ge0$, $W\ge X+Y-1$, $W\le X$, and $W\le Y$.

Every defining bound and McCormick inequality is affine in $(x,y,w)$. If two points satisfy one such affine inequality, their line segment also satisfies it by linearity, so the polytope is convex by [F2]. By step 1.1 every graph point lies in this polytope, and therefore each finite convex combination of graph points lies there by repeated segment closure [L1].

If $u_x=l_x$, the first lower and first upper inequalities force $w=l_xy$; all graph points satisfy the other inequalities by step 1.1. For any $y,y'\in[l_y,u_y]$ and $\theta\in[0,1]$, the segment between $(l_x,y,l_xy)$ and $(l_x,y',l_xy')$ is $(l_x,\theta y+(1-\theta)y',l_x(\theta y+(1-\theta)y'))$, again on the graph. If $u_y=l_y$, the first lower and second upper inequalities force $w=x l_y$, and the same calculation with $x,x'\in[l_x,u_x]$ proves convexity. Thus either degenerate case gives the product graph itself.

In the nondegenerate case of step 1.2, set $\lambda_{11}=W$, $\lambda_{10}=X-W$, $\lambda_{01}=Y-W$, and $\lambda_{00}=1-X-Y+W$. Step 1.2 makes each coefficient nonnegative; their sum is $1$, and $(X,Y,W)=\lambda_{00}(0,0,0)+\lambda_{10}(1,0,0)+\lambda_{01}(0,1,0)+\lambda_{11}(1,1,1)$. Each vertex lies on $W=XY$, so every normalized polytope point is a convex combination of graph points.

If either width is zero, step 2.2 gives equality directly. If both are positive, the affine map in step 1.2 is invertible, and steps 2.1 and 2.3 prove both inclusions after normalization. These cases exhaust the ordered endpoint choices, proving equality of the original polytope and graph convex hull.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Input a candidate list $X=(c_1,\ldots,c_M)$, a horizon $N$, an initial-list length $s$, a real-mean candidate $m$, a kernel candidate $k$, an observation-variance candidate $\sigma^2$, coefficients $(b_t)_{0\le t<N}$, an initial data list $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^s$, an observation oracle $O$, and a selector that is either the exact rule below or a certified approximate rule below. For $N=0$, the coefficient list is empty. First validate that $X$ is nonempty, finite, and ordered; $N$ and $s$ are integers with $N\ge0$ and $0\le s\le N$; every initial site lies in $X$; all mean, kernel, noise, coefficient, and initial-observation values are finite reals; the kernel matrix on $X$ is symmetric positive semidefinite; $\sigma^2\ge0$; and each required $b_t$ is defined and nonnegative. If any validation fails, return `inadmissible-model` before computing a posterior. The observation oracle must finish each call in finite time and return either a finite real observation or `observation-unavailable`. For a true-posterior interpretation, the initial sites are fixed before their observations and each observation is $f(x_i)+\xi_i$ under this model, with errors independent centered Gaussian variables of variance $\sigma^2$ and independent of the entire process. In this interpretation, whether a call returns a value or `observation-unavailable` must be a deterministic measurable function of the already observed history and selected site, decided without inspecting the unobserved process or the fresh noise; thus availability conveys no additional information. Otherwise the procedure computes only the all-data-vector posterior kernel for the specified surrogate and makes no claim that it is the conditional law of an externally supplied data-generating process. The Axiom of Choice is included as required by [[thm-finite-gaussian-process-posterior-and-predictive-laws]].

Denote the sites in the accumulated observation trace, in observation order, by $x_1,\ldots,x_t$; these are not the candidate-list indices and may repeat. Write $X_t=(x_1,\ldots,x_t)$, $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_t)$, $m_{X_t}=(m(x_i))_{i\le t}$, and $k_t(x)=(k(x_i,x))_{i\le t}$. Initialize the trace with the given data and let its length be $t=s$. If $C_t$ is not certified positive definite, or its Cholesky factorization or required solves are unavailable, return `posterior-solve-unavailable` with the initial trace and no posterior state. Otherwise compute the current posterior by the formulas below. At every later history length $t\ge1$, use the same rule to compute its state immediately after the new observation is appended. Never use a pseudoinverse or clip a negative variance. In particular, this state update is performed after the final observation at history length $N$, before a `complete` return.

If the initialized history already has length $t=N$, return `complete` with the initial trace, its computed posterior state, and the empty list of acquisition errors. Otherwise $t<N$, and for each candidate compute
$$\mu_t(x)=m(x)+k_t(x)^T C_t^{-1}(y-m_{X_t})$$
$$v_t(x)=k(x,x)-k_t(x)^T C_t^{-1}k_t(x),\qquad s_t(x)=\sqrt{v_t(x)}$$
where the observed covariance and solves satisfy the hypotheses of [[thm-finite-gaussian-process-posterior-and-predictive-laws]]. At $t=0$, use the prior formulas above. At $t\ge1$, its conditional covariance is positive semidefinite, so $v_t(x)\ge0$; [[thm-of-square-roots]] supplies the unique nonnegative square root used here. If nonnegativity of a computed $v_t(x)$ cannot be verified, return `posterior-solve-unavailable` with the current trace and last valid state. derivations.claim: At the initial history, no adaptive observations have yet been added; if the supplied fixed initial list is empty, the conditional law is the given GP prior, and otherwise [F1] gives its posterior whenever its observed covariance is positive definite. The algorithm computes that initial state before any acquisition, and the all-data-vector posterior version in [F1] fixes the kernel for every possible observed value.

Assume as the induction hypothesis that the posterior formula is valid after a finite history $H_t$. By [F3], the next candidate index is a measurable function of $H_t$, so conditioning on the selected site adds no information beyond $H_t$. Observation availability is already determined by $H_t$ and that site, so a successful response adds no further selection information. Thus the new noisy observation is a Gaussian coordinate of this conditional vector plus independent Gaussian noise. The observed covariance of the augmented list is positive definite; when $t\ge1$, its scalar conditional variance is the positive Schur complement of $C_t$ in $C_{t+1}$, and when $t=0$ it is the positive observed variance in $C_1$. Input a compact-box instance $(D_0,C,f)$ from [[def-spatial-global-optimization-problem]], a tolerance $\varepsilon>0$, a positive integer node budget $N$, and a deterministic box-report oracle implementing [[def-spatial-box-bound-certificate]]. Every oracle call must finish in finite time or return an unavailable status. The budget counts each oracle call, including the root and both children after every split. The oracle may request higher precision on a repeated box; each such refinement is another counted call.

Initialize a leaf ledger with the root box $D_0$, no incumbent ($U=+\infty$), and zero calls. Evaluate the root first. Before every oracle call, if the call counter is already $N$, return the complete current ledger with budget-exhausted; otherwise call the oracle and increment the counter by one. Store every returned field. A feasible witness $(x,U_x)$ updates the incumbent upper bound to $U=\min U_x$. An empty-box proof marks that leaf empty; retain the leaf and its proof in the ledger, but exclude it from lower-bound comparisons, closure tests, and split candidates. For constraints $g_i(x)\le0$, a sound interval lower bound $\underline g_i(B)>0$ is an empty-box proof. Store every valid lower bound $\ell_B$ even if the leaf is later closed. Every evaluated leaf not certified empty requires a finite lower bound; if that field is missing, non-finite, or unavailable, return inconclusive. A certified-empty leaf requires no lower bound.

Whenever all current leaves have been evaluated, first return infeasible if they are all certified empty. Otherwise put $L=\min\{\ell_B:B\text{ is not certified empty}\}$. If $U<+\infty$, $L$ is finite, and $U-L\le\varepsilon$, return a feasible witness and the epsilon-global certificate $(L,U)$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then:

1. If $(X,d_X)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]), the image
   $f[X] \subseteq Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$.
2. More generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$, then $f[K]$ is
   a compact subset of $Y$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $K \subseteq X$ be a
compact subset ([[def-metric-compactness]]). Then $K$ is closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

No choice principle is used: both covers below are given by a rule, and the
indexed form of [[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]] returns indices rather than
sets.

**The converse is false in general.** A closed and bounded subset of an arbitrary
metric space need not be compact
([[fs-closed-and-bounded-implies-compact-in-every-metric-space]]); it is exactly
in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that the converse holds ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below. Then $S$ has a
greatest lower bound in $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-infimum]]), and it is given by

$$\inf S = -\sup(-S), \qquad \text{where } -S = \{-s : s \in S\}.$$

In particular the complete ordered field $\mathbb{R}$ has the
greatest-lower-bound property, which is therefore not an extra axiom: it is a
consequence of the least-upper-bound property.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below, and let $\ell$ be a
lower bound of $S$ ([[def-bounded-set]]). Then

$$\ell = \inf S \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \text{for every } \varepsilon > 0 \text{ there exists } s \in S \text{ with } s < \ell + \varepsilon.$$

In words: among the lower bounds of $S$, the infimum is exactly the one that
cannot be raised by any positive amount and still bound $S$ from below.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $A \subseteq X$,
with closure, derived set and limit points as in
[[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]. Then:

1. If $A \ne \emptyset$, then $\overline{A} = \{\, x \in X : d(x,A) = 0 \,\}$,
   where $d(x,A)$ is the distance from a point to a nonempty set
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
2. $\overline{A} = A \cup A'$.
3. $\overline{A}$ is closed, contains $A$, and is contained in every closed
   $F \subseteq X$ with $A \subseteq F$. So $\overline{A}$ is the smallest closed
   superset of $A$, and $A$ is closed if and only if $A = \overline{A}$.

Claims 2 and 3 hold for every $A$, the empty set included: $\overline{\emptyset}$
is empty because no ball meets $\emptyset$, and $\emptyset$ is closed because $X$
is open ([[def-metric-topology]]). Claim 1 carries the hypothesis $A \ne \emptyset$
because $d(x,A)$ is defined only for nonempty $A$
([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

Define $d_{\mathbb{R}} : \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) := |x - y|$ ([[def-abs-value]]). Then:

1. $d_{\mathbb{R}}$ is a metric on $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-metric-space]]); it is
   called the **usual metric** of $\mathbb{R}$.
2. For $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and $r > 0$ the open ball is the bounded open interval
   ([[def-interval]], [[def-metric-ball]])
   $$B(x,r) = (x-r,\ x+r),$$
   and the closed ball is $\bar B(x,r) = [x-r,\ x+r]$.
3. Consequently $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is open in the metric topology of
   $d_{\mathbb{R}}$ ([[def-metric-topology]]) exactly when for every $x \in U$
   there is $r > 0$ with $(x-r, x+r) \subseteq U$. This topology is called the
   **usual topology** of $\mathbb{R}$.
4. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ is not a bounded metric space
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]): no ball contains $\mathbb{R}$, so
   $\operatorname{diam}(\mathbb{R})$ is not defined.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$A, B \subseteq X$.

**Bounded subset.** $A$ is **bounded** if $A = \emptyset$ or there are $x_0 \in X$
and a real $r > 0$ with $A \subseteq B(x_0, r)$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). The space
$(X,d)$ is a **bounded metric space** if $X$ is a bounded subset of itself.

**Diameter, for nonempty bounded $A$ only.** Suppose $A$ is nonempty and
bounded, and put

$$D(A) := \{\, d(a,b) : a, b \in A \,\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}.$$

Then $D(A)$ is nonempty, since $A$ is, and it is bounded above: fixing $x_0$ and
$r$ with $A \subseteq B(x_0,r)$, every $a, b \in A$ satisfy
$d(a,b) \le d(a,x_0) + d(x_0,b) < r + r$ by the triangle inequality, symmetry
([[def-metric-space]]) and addition of inequalities ([[lem-of-add-order]],
[[def-ordered-field]]), so $r + r$ is an upper bound of $D(A)$
([[def-bounded-set]]). Hence $D(A)$ has a least upper bound in $\mathbb{R}$ by
the least-upper-bound property ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), and that bound
is unique ([[lem-sup-unique]]). Define

$$\operatorname{diam}(A) := \sup D(A).$$

**Distance from a point to a set, for nonempty $A$ only.** Let $x \in X$ and let
$A$ be nonempty, and put $E(x,A) := \{\, d(x,a) : a \in A \,\}$. Then $E(x,A)$ is
nonempty and bounded below by $0$, since a metric is nonnegative
([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]], [[def-bounded-set]]), so it has a greatest lower
bound ([[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]]), unique by [[lem-sup-unique]].
Define

$$d(x,A) := \inf E(x,A).$$

**Distance between two sets, for nonempty $A$ and $B$ only.** Put
$E(A,B) := \{\, d(a,b) : a \in A,\ b \in B \,\}$, again nonempty and bounded
below by $0$, and define

$$d(A,B) := \inf E(A,B).$$

**Every one of the three scope restrictions is load bearing.** In this library
$\sup$ and $\inf$ denote real numbers and are written only after existence has
been established; the least-upper-bound property of [[def-complete-ordered-field]] and the
greatest-lower-bound property of [[thm-infimum-property]] apply to nonempty
real sets with the respective bounds. Empty or unbounded sets acquire no
real supremum or infimum by convention. Accordingly:

- $\operatorname{diam}(A)$ is defined exactly when $A$ is nonempty **and**
  bounded. It is not defined for $A = \emptyset$, and it is not defined, not even
  as an infinite value, for an unbounded $A$.
- $d(x,A)$ is defined exactly when $A \ne \emptyset$, and $d(A,B)$ exactly when
  both $A$ and $B$ are nonempty. No boundedness is needed for these two, because
  $0$ is always a lower bound.

For each $k \in \mathbb{N}$ let $I_k = [a_k, b_k]$ be a closed bounded interval
with $a_k \le b_k$ ([[def-interval]]), and suppose the family is **nested**:

$$I_{k+1} \subseteq I_k \qquad (k \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $\ell_k = b_k - a_k \ge 0$ for the length of $I_k$. Then:

1. $\displaystyle\bigcap_{k \in \mathbb{N}} I_k$ is **nonempty**. More precisely,
   with $a = \sup\{a_k : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$ and
   $b = \inf\{b_k : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$, both of which exist, one has $a \le b$
   and $$\bigcap_{k \in \mathbb{N}} I_k = [a, b].$$
2. $\displaystyle\bigcap_{k \in \mathbb{N}} I_k$ is a **single point** if and only
   if $\ell_k \to 0$ ([[def-real-limit]]).

empty; dropping boundedness does the same; and dropping nonemptiness of the
individual intervals is vacuously fatal.

derivations.claim: The box $D_0$ is nonempty (its left-endpoint vector belongs to it) and compact by [F1]. Therefore $f[D_0]$ is nonempty and compact by [F2], hence closed and bounded. By the boundedness definition and [F5], there are $c\in\mathbb R$ and $r>0$ such that $f[D_0]\subseteq(c-r,c+r)$, so $c-r$ is a lower bound. Let $f^*=\inf f[D_0]$, which exists by [F3]. For every $\eta>0$, [F3] gives $y\in f[D_0]$ with $f^*\le y<f^*+\eta$; by [F5] every open ball around $f^*$ meets $f[D_0]$. Thus $f^*\in\overline{f[D_0]}$ by [F4], and closedness gives $f^*\in f[D_0]$. So $f$ attains its minimum on $D_0$, and every feasible objective value is at least $f^*$.

The incumbent upper bounds $U_k$ are nonincreasing, and each is at least the attained minimum $f^*$ by step 1.1 and [A2]. If the unlimited continuation did not terminate, it would expand infinitely many boxes. The expansion tree is binary, so there is an infinite nested branch: recursively take the left child if it has infinitely many expanded descendants and otherwise take the right child. This rule is deterministic and requires no choice principle.

Along this branch, longest-side bisection makes every side length tend to zero. Fix $\eta>0$. Each coordinate can be halved only finitely many times while its side length is at least $\eta$, because each halving divides a finite initial length by two and never increases it. There are finitely many coordinates, and every split whose box has a side of length at least $\eta$ halves one such longest side, so only finitely many such splits occur. Thus the maximum side length tends to zero. The nested closed coordinate intervals have a unique common point in each coordinate by [F7], giving $x\in D_0$.

Let $U_k$ be the incumbent at the split checkpoint at which branch box $B_k$ is expanded. The closure test has already been applied, so [F6] gives $\ell(B_k)<U_k-\varepsilon$. That box was previously evaluated at its midpoint $m_k$, so [A2] and the incumbent update give $U_k\le f(m_k)$. By step 3.1, $m_k\to x$; continuity and consistency [A1] imply $f(m_k)\to f(x)$ and $\ell(B_k)\to f(x)$. Thus $\ell(B_k)<f(m_k)-\varepsilon$ for every $k$, whose limit gives $f(x)\le f(x)-\varepsilon$, contradicting $\varepsilon>0$.

Thus the unlimited continuation cannot expand infinitely many boxes without meeting $U-L\le\varepsilon$. It reaches that certificate after finitely many calls, so any larger finite call budget returns it.

A finite **factorable expression DAG** on a box $B$ has input variables, certified constants, affine nodes, product nodes, and optional unary nonlinear nodes. A **certified convex relaxation** of its constrained minimization problem consists of a convex-program representation in the form of [[def-convex-program-duality-and-slater-condition]], with feasible set $R_B$ in lifted variables and convex objective $\phi_B$ on $R_B$, and an exact-value embedding $\iota_B$ with these properties:

1. For every original feasible point $x\in B\cap C$, the exact value of each DAG node defines $\iota_B(x)\in R_B$.
2. The relaxed objective underestimates the original: $\phi_B(\iota_B(x))\le f(x)$.
3. Every product node $w=uv$ is represented by a McCormick polytope from [[def-mccormick-bilinear-box-envelope]] using operand bounds that enclose their exact ranges. Every other nonlinear node must use supplied convex and concave graph enclosures with verified domain hypotheses. If no such enclosure is supplied, no relaxation is defined.
4. Every interval bound and coefficient affected by finite precision carries an outward-rounded enclosure from [[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]. A non-finite status or unverified coefficient makes the relaxation unavailable.

For a convex program represented in [[def-convex-program-duality-and-slater-condition]], a dual certificate is a dual-feasible pair $(\lambda,\nu)$ together with a verified real lower bound $\ell$ for its Lagrangian dual value $q(\lambda,\nu)$. The definition records a certificate interface only; it does not assert that a solver finds one.

For every finite box $[l_x,u_x]\times[l_y,u_y]$, the McCormick polytope from [[def-mccormick-bilinear-box-envelope]] is exactly the convex hull in $\mathbb R^3$ of the graph $\{(x,y,xy):x\in[l_x,u_x],y\in[l_y,u_y]\}$.

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or
`inconclusive` status makes no finite claim. For a finite expression DAG
whose operation nodes all return finite enclosures, every exact node value
from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any
node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

For the convex program and Lagrangian dual of
[[def-convex-program-duality-and-slater-condition]], every primal feasible
$x$ and every dual feasible $(\lambda,\nu)$ satisfy
$$q(\lambda,\nu)\le f_0(x).$$
Consequently, when the primal feasible set is nonempty, $d^*\le p^*$.

Every other nonlinear relation is included only with a verified outer graph enclosure by the algorithm definition. Thus the constructed lifted point $\iota_B(x)$ lies in $R_B$, and the relaxed objective satisfies $\phi_B(\iota_B(x))\le f(x)$ by [F1].

Weak duality [F4], applied to the relaxed primal point $\iota_B(x)$ from step 1.1, gives $q(\lambda,\nu)\le\phi_B(\iota_B(x))$. Since the verified certificate satisfies $\ell\le q(\lambda,\nu)$, we obtain $\ell\le\phi_B(\iota_B(x))\le f(x)$.

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or
`inconclusive` status makes no finite claim. For a finite expression DAG
whose operation nodes all return finite enclosures, every exact node value
from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any
node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

For finite $x$ with $|x|\le N_{\max}$, the directed roundings defined in
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]] satisfy
$\operatorname{rd}(x)\le x\le\operatorname{ru}(x)$ and each endpoint error is
at most the stated $\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)$ (with zero error when $x$ is
representable). For $x>N_{\max}$ the pair $(N_{\max},+\infty)$ encloses $x$;
for $x<-N_{\max}$ the pair $(-\infty,-N_{\max})$ encloses $x$. Overflow has
error bound $+\infty$ and cannot be reported as a finite-error result.

An exact dyadic rational is a number $m2^q$ with integers $m,q$.
Fix integers $p\ge2$ and $e_{\min}\le e_{\max}$. Put
$\eta=2^{e_{\min}-p+1}$ and
$N_{\max}=(2^p-1)2^{e_{\max}-p+1}$. The finite representable set $\mathbb F$
consists of zero, both signs of every normal number $k2^{e-p+1}$ with integers $e,k$ satisfying
$e_{\min}\le e\le e_{\max}$ and $2^{p-1}\le k<2^p$, and both signs of every
subnormal number $k\eta$ with integer $k$ satisfying $1\le k<2^{p-1}$. The smallest positive
subnormal is $\eta$, the smallest positive normal is $2^{e_{\min}}$, and the
largest finite magnitude is $N_{\max}$. The extended endpoint set also contains
$-\infty$ and $+\infty$ as enclosure sentinels; they are not finite machine
numbers.

For a real $x$ with $|x|\le N_{\max}$, define $\operatorname{rd}(x)$ as the
greatest member of $\mathbb F$ not exceeding $x$, and $\operatorname{ru}(x)$ as
the least member of $\mathbb F$ not less than $x$. Define
$\rho(x)=\operatorname{ru}(x)-\operatorname{rd}(x)$. Set $\epsilon_{\rm abs}(0)=0$.
For nonzero $x$ in the
subnormal range, define the absolute-error bound $\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)=\eta$;
for $2^e\le |x|<2^{e+1}$ in the normal range, define
$\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)=2^{e-p+2}$. For $x>N_{\max}$, set
$(\operatorname{rd}(x),\operatorname{ru}(x))=(N_{\max},+\infty)$; for
$x<-N_{\max}$, set
$(\operatorname{rd}(x),\operatorname{ru}(x))=(-\infty,-N_{\max})$.
In either overflow case set $\epsilon_{\rm abs}(x)=+\infty$ and report
`overflow`, even when the selected directed endpoint is finite.
The rounding procedure reports `finite`, `subnormal`, or
`overflow`, so no relative-error assumption is implicit.

An exact rational intermediate may be converted by comparing integer
numerators and denominators after clearing powers of two. A directed interval
endpoint is the resulting greatest lower or least upper member of the
extended endpoint set $\mathbb F\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\}$.

Input a box $B=\prod_j[a_j,b_j]\subseteq D_0$ with arbitrary finite ordered real endpoints, a finite real expression DAG from [[def-intervals-rectangles-and-complex-balls]] using addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division, a precision $p\ge2$, and a dyadic format with fixed exponent bounds. Round each input endpoint outward at precision $p$, replacing $[a_j,b_j]$ by $[\operatorname{rd}_p(a_j),\operatorname{ru}_p(b_j)]$; if an endpoint rounding overflows, return overflow. Thus every interval passed to an interval operation has dyadic endpoints and contains the original box coordinate interval. The same rule applies to a singleton input, including a midpoint point-evaluation path. The DAG must define a real-valued function at every point of $B$; for each division node its denominator range on $B$ must exclude zero. Each constant is either an exact dyadic, enclosed by $[\operatorname{rd}_p(c),\operatorname{ru}_p(c)]$, or is accompanied by a precision-indexed certified interval containing it whose width tends to zero as $p\to\infty$. If any constant enclosure overflows or is unavailable, return that status with no finite bound claim. Traverse the finite DAG in topological order. Enclose each input by its outward-rounded interval, each constant by its certified interval at precision $p$, and apply the corresponding outward-rounded operation from [[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] at precision $p$. Return the root enclosure $I_p(B)=[a_-,a_+]$, its lower and upper endpoints, and the exact midpoint of $B$ as a candidate point. If any operation returns overflow, split-domain, domain-error, entire, or inconclusive, return that status with no finite bound claim.

For a continuous objective on an unconstrained box, the midpoint is feasible and $a_+$ is a verified upper bound for its objective value. On a constrained box, the midpoint is only a candidate: a separate feasibility witness is required. To refine arithmetic error, callers increase $p$ along any sequence of shrinking boxes. Fixed exponent bounds must be chosen so no exact intermediate on the certified domain overflows; otherwise the procedure returns an explicit failure status.

A **real interval** is a closed set $[a,b]\subset\mathbb R$ with finite dyadic
endpoints $a\le b$. Its width is $b-a$, midpoint is $(a+b)/2$, and its
midpoint-radius form is $m+[-r,r]$ with $m=(a+b)/2$ and $r=(b-a)/2$. The empty
set is the status `empty`; the whole real line is `entire`. `overflow`,
`domain-error`, `split-domain`, and `inconclusive` are computation statuses,
not finite intervals.

A **complex rectangle** is $X+iY=\{x+iy:x\in X,\ y\in Y\}$ for real intervals
$X,Y$. Complex addition and multiplication use
$(x+iy)+(u+iv)=(x+u)+i(y+v)$ and
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$. For $z=x+iy$, its complex modulus is
$|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$, and for $z\ne0$ its reciprocal is
$1/z=(x-iy)/(x^2+y^2)$. A
**complex ball** $B(c,r)$ is
$\{z\in\mathbb C:|z-c|\le r\}$ with dyadic complex center $c$ and dyadic
$r\ge0$. For any two represented sets $S,T$, the inclusion order is
$S\sqsubseteq T$ iff $S\subseteq T$.

The width of a complex rectangle with coordinate widths $w_X,w_Y$ is its
Euclidean diameter $\sqrt{w_X^2+w_Y^2}$; the width of a ball $B(c,r)$ is its
diameter $2r$. Width comparisons against a dyadic tolerance can be decided by
exact rational comparisons after squaring the nonnegative quantities.

The **range** of a real or complex function $f$ on a set $S$ is
$f(S)=\{f(x):x\in S\cap\operatorname{dom}(f)\}$. A finite expression DAG is a
finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes, constant nodes, and operation
nodes; constants are exact dyadics or are supplied with certified enclosing
intervals. Sharing a node means the exact same intermediate value is reused.

For real intervals $X=[a,b]$ and $Y=[c,d]$, compute the displayed exact
endpoint formulas and round the lower endpoint down and the upper endpoint up
in the format of
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. If either exact
endpoint overflows, return `overflow` with the outward extended endpoints;
never substitute a finite endpoint for an overflow sentinel. Addition is
$[a+c,b+d]$, subtraction is $[a-d,b-c]$, and multiplication is
$[\min(ac,ad,bc,bd),\max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]$. Division is defined only when
$0\notin Y$ and is $X[1/d,1/c]$, with reciprocal endpoints computed as exact
rationals before outward rounding. Squaring is
$[0,\max(a^2,b^2)]$ when $0\in X$ and
$[\min(a^2,b^2),\max(a^2,b^2)]$ otherwise. Square root is defined only for
$X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and is enclosed by applying
[[alg-dyadic-square-root-bisection]] to the exact dyadic endpoints with
request $n=p$, where $p$ is the selected format precision, and rounding
outward for storage.

Input a compact-box instance $(D_0,C,f)$, a finite arithmetic expression DAG representing $f$, a closed box $B=\prod_{j=1}^n[a_j,b_j]\subseteq D_0$, a nonnegative certified constant $L$, a precision $p\ge2$, a dyadic interval format with fixed exponent bounds, a certificate that the midpoint $m$ is in $C$ (automatic when $C=D_0$), and a validated inequality
$$|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\max_j|x_j-y_j|\qquad(x,y\in B).$$
Let $m_j=(a_j+b_j)/2$ and $r=\max_j(b_j-a_j)/2$. Apply [[alg-interval-dag-box-enclosure-and-bound]] to the supplied DAG at the singleton $\{m\}$ with the supplied precision and format to obtain $I_p(\{m\})=[q_-,q_+]$; its endpoint-rounding rule encloses a possibly non-dyadic midpoint. Compute a directed-rounding upper bound $r^+\ge r$ and a downward-rounded lower endpoint $\ell_B\le q_- - Lr^+$. Return the pointwise lower-bound report $\ell_B$ and the feasible midpoint candidate $(m,q_+)$. If the feasibility certificate or either interval or arithmetic calculation is unavailable or non-finite, return inconclusive without a feasible-witness claim.

derivations.claim: By the endpoint-rounding rule and [F2], the dyadic input intervals used by the algorithm contain the original box $B$. The DAG enclosure statement [F1] therefore implies $a_-\le f(x)\le a_+$ for every $x\in B$. Thus $a_-$ and $a_+$ are valid lower and upper bounds on the entire box, not estimates from a sample point.

For a nested shrinking sequence $B_k\to\{x\}$ with precision $p_k\to\infty$, outward-rounded input endpoints tend to their exact endpoint values by [F2], and each certified constant enclosure tends to its exact constant by the hypothesis. Induct in topological order through the finite DAG. At each addition, subtraction, or multiplication node the exact endpoint formulas are continuous in the input endpoints; at a division node the denominator is bounded away from zero, so the reciprocal endpoint formulas are continuous for all sufficiently large $k$. The directed-rounding error tends to zero by [F2]. Therefore each node enclosure converges to its exact node value at $x$, and in particular the root endpoints converge to $f(x)$.
For the Lipschitz procedure, every $x\in B$ satisfies $\max_j|x_j-m_j|\le r\le r^+$. By [F4], $f(x)\ge f(m)-Lr\ge q_- - Lr^+\ge\ell_B$, so $\ell_B$ is valid on $B$.

Along a shrinking sequence, $m_k\to x$, $r_k^+\to0$, and the singleton enclosure endpoints $q_{k,-},q_{k,+}$ tend to $f(x)$ by step 1.2. Hence $q_{k,-}-Lr_k^+\to f(x)$, and the extra directed-rounding error also tends to zero by [F2]; therefore $\ell_{B_k}\to f(x)$.

A **box** in $\mathbb R^n$ is $D_0=\prod_{j=1}^n[a_j,b_j]$ with finite real endpoints $a_j\le b_j$. Here $n\ge1$. The box is closed and bounded, hence compact by [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]. An **optimization instance on a compact box** consists of this $D_0$, a continuous objective $f:D_0\to\mathbb R$ (continuity in the inherited Euclidean metric, as in [[def-metric-continuity]]), and a feasible set $C\subseteq D_0$. The unconstrained instance has $C=D_0$. A constrained instance may specify $C=\{x\in D_0:g_i(x)\le0,\ 1\le i\le m\}$ for a finite list of real functions $g_i$.

When $C\ne\emptyset$, the set $f[C]$ is nonempty and bounded below: $D_0$ is compact by [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], its continuous image $f[D_0]$ is compact in the usual metric on $\mathbb R$ by [[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]] and therefore bounded by [[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]. Thus $f[D_0]$ lies in a real interval $(c-r,c+r)$ for some $c\in\mathbb R$ and $r>0$, by [[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]; hence $c-r$ is a lower bound of $f[C]\subseteq f[D_0]$. Therefore [[thm-infimum-property]] gives the real number $f^*=\inf f[C]$, using [[def-infimum]]. No attainment is assumed for a general $C$. Statements about finite empty-set detection require a separate constraint certificate or a stated separation margin; objective continuity alone does not certify infeasibility.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then:

1. If $(X,d_X)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]), the image
   $f[X] \subseteq Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$.
2. More generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$, then $f[K]$ is
   a compact subset of $Y$.

No choice principle is used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $K \subseteq X$ be a
compact subset ([[def-metric-compactness]]). Then $K$ is closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

No choice principle is used: both covers below are given by a rule, and the
indexed form of [[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]] returns indices rather than
sets.

**The converse is false in general.** A closed and bounded subset of an arbitrary
metric space need not be compact
([[fs-closed-and-bounded-implies-compact-in-every-metric-space]]); it is exactly
in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that the converse holds ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the
set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: [[lem-finite-subsets-listable]] proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of
**real** numbers from this page onwards.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $m \in \mathbb{R}$.

- $m$ is a **maximum** (or *greatest element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $s \le m$
  for every $s \in S$.
- $m$ is a **minimum** (or *least element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $m \le s$
  for every $s \in S$.

A set has at most one maximum: if $m_1$ and $m_2$ are both maxima then
$m_1 \in S$ gives $m_1 \le m_2$ and $m_2 \in S$ gives $m_2 \le m_1$, so
$m_1 = m_2$ by antisymmetry of the order, which is immediate from the trichotomy
axiom of an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]]).
The same argument applies to minima, so we may write $\max S$ and $\min S$.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below. Then $S$ has a
greatest lower bound in $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-infimum]]), and it is given by

$$\inf S = -\sup(-S), \qquad \text{where } -S = \{-s : s \in S\}.$$

In particular the complete ordered field $\mathbb{R}$ has the
greatest-lower-bound property, which is therefore not an extra axiom: it is a
consequence of the least-upper-bound property.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below, and let $\ell$ be a
lower bound of $S$ ([[def-bounded-set]]). Then

$$\ell = \inf S \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \text{for every } \varepsilon > 0 \text{ there exists } s \in S \text{ with } s < \ell + \varepsilon.$$

In words: among the lower bounds of $S$, the infimum is exactly the one that
cannot be raised by any positive amount and still bound $S$ from below.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $A \subseteq X$,
with closure, derived set and limit points as in
[[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]. Then:

1. If $A \ne \emptyset$, then $\overline{A} = \{\, x \in X : d(x,A) = 0 \,\}$,
   where $d(x,A)$ is the distance from a point to a nonempty set
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
2. $\overline{A} = A \cup A'$.
3. $\overline{A}$ is closed, contains $A$, and is contained in every closed
   $F \subseteq X$ with $A \subseteq F$. So $\overline{A}$ is the smallest closed
   superset of $A$, and $A$ is closed if and only if $A = \overline{A}$.

Claims 2 and 3 hold for every $A$, the empty set included: $\overline{\emptyset}$
is empty because no ball meets $\emptyset$, and $\emptyset$ is closed because $X$
is open ([[def-metric-topology]]). Claim 1 carries the hypothesis $A \ne \emptyset$
because $d(x,A)$ is defined only for nonempty $A$
([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

Define $d_{\mathbb{R}} : \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) := |x - y|$ ([[def-abs-value]]). Then:

1. $d_{\mathbb{R}}$ is a metric on $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-metric-space]]); it is
   called the **usual metric** of $\mathbb{R}$.
2. For $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and $r > 0$ the open ball is the bounded open interval
   ([[def-interval]], [[def-metric-ball]])
   $$B(x,r) = (x-r,\ x+r),$$
   and the closed ball is $\bar B(x,r) = [x-r,\ x+r]$.
3. Consequently $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is open in the metric topology of
   $d_{\mathbb{R}}$ ([[def-metric-topology]]) exactly when for every $x \in U$
   there is $r > 0$ with $(x-r, x+r) \subseteq U$. This topology is called the
   **usual topology** of $\mathbb{R}$.
4. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ is not a bounded metric space
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]): no ball contains $\mathbb{R}$, so
   $\operatorname{diam}(\mathbb{R})$ is not defined.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$A, B \subseteq X$.

**Bounded subset.** $A$ is **bounded** if $A = \emptyset$ or there are $x_0 \in X$
and a real $r > 0$ with $A \subseteq B(x_0, r)$ ([[def-metric-ball]]). The space
$(X,d)$ is a **bounded metric space** if $X$ is a bounded subset of itself.

**Diameter, for nonempty bounded $A$ only.** Suppose $A$ is nonempty and
bounded, and put

$$D(A) := \{\, d(a,b) : a, b \in A \,\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}.$$

Then $D(A)$ is nonempty, since $A$ is, and it is bounded above: fixing $x_0$ and
$r$ with $A \subseteq B(x_0,r)$, every $a, b \in A$ satisfy
$d(a,b) \le d(a,x_0) + d(x_0,b) < r + r$ by the triangle inequality, symmetry
([[def-metric-space]]) and addition of inequalities ([[lem-of-add-order]],
[[def-ordered-field]]), so $r + r$ is an upper bound of $D(A)$
([[def-bounded-set]]). Hence $D(A)$ has a least upper bound in $\mathbb{R}$ by
the least-upper-bound property ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), and that bound
is unique ([[lem-sup-unique]]). Define

$$\operatorname{diam}(A) := \sup D(A).$$

**Distance from a point to a set, for nonempty $A$ only.** Let $x \in X$ and let
$A$ be nonempty, and put $E(x,A) := \{\, d(x,a) : a \in A \,\}$. Then $E(x,A)$ is
nonempty and bounded below by $0$, since a metric is nonnegative
([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]], [[def-bounded-set]]), so it has a greatest lower
bound ([[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]]), unique by [[lem-sup-unique]].
Define

$$d(x,A) := \inf E(x,A).$$

**Distance between two sets, for nonempty $A$ and $B$ only.** Put
$E(A,B) := \{\, d(a,b) : a \in A,\ b \in B \,\}$, again nonempty and bounded
below by $0$, and define

$$d(A,B) := \inf E(A,B).$$

**Every one of the three scope restrictions is load bearing.** In this library
$\sup$ and $\inf$ denote real numbers and are written only after existence has
been established; the least-upper-bound property of [[def-complete-ordered-field]] and the
greatest-lower-bound property of [[thm-infimum-property]] apply to nonempty
real sets with the respective bounds. Empty or unbounded sets acquire no
real supremum or infimum by convention. Accordingly:

- $\operatorname{diam}(A)$ is defined exactly when $A$ is nonempty **and**
  bounded. It is not defined for $A = \emptyset$, and it is not defined, not even
  as an infinite value, for an unbounded $A$.
- $d(x,A)$ is defined exactly when $A \ne \emptyset$, and $d(A,B)$ exactly when
  both $A$ and $B$ are nonempty. No boundedness is needed for these two, because
  $0$ is always a lower bound.

Input a nonempty box $D_0$ from [[def-spatial-global-optimization-problem]], a finite nonempty list of constraints $g_i(x)\le0$, a positive integer query budget $N$, and a deterministic oracle returning a sound lower bound $\ell_i(B)\le\inf_{x\in B}g_i(x)$ for every queried box. The oracle returns explicit unavailable or non-finite statuses when it cannot certify a finite bound. For a valid arithmetic-DAG oracle as in [[thm-interval-lipschitz-bound-sound-consistent]], choose one fixed exponent range large enough to avoid overflow and set the query precision to $p_0+d+r$, where $p_0\ge2$, $d$ is the split depth, and $r\ge0$ is a singleton-refinement index.

Initialize a FIFO queue with $(D_0,0,0)$ and an empty ledger. Each oracle query consumes one unit, including a singleton precision refinement. Before a query, if the budget is exhausted, return the current queue and ledger with `budget-exhausted`. Query all $g_i$, in index order, on the oldest queued box at precision $p_0+d+r$; this one box query requests the vector of constraint bounds and consumes one budget unit. If any reported bound is unavailable or has a non-finite status, return `inconclusive` with the current queue and ledger, without an emptiness claim. Otherwise record the finite lower bounds and remove that entry from the queue. If some $\ell_i(B)>0$, record the box as certified empty. If no lower bound is positive and $B$ has positive width, bisect a longest coordinate at its exact midpoint, using the least coordinate index to break ties, and enqueue the two closed children, lower half first and upper half second, at depth $d+1$ with refinement index $0$. If $B$ is a singleton with no positive lower bound, enqueue the same point with split depth $d$ and refinement index $r+1$, so its next query uses strictly higher precision. When the queue is empty, return `infeasible` with the complete ledger. This procedure has no termination claim without an additional separation condition; it returns infeasible only from a finite cover by certified-empty boxes.

Assume a finite arithmetic expression DAG uses $+$, $-$, $\times$, and division only where the exact denominator is bounded away from zero on the box. Each constant is an exact dyadic or has certified enclosures at precision $p$ whose widths tend to zero as $p\to\infty$. Assume all operation results are finite. For every precision $p$, the enclosure returned by [[alg-interval-dag-box-enclosure-and-bound]] contains the exact range $f[B]$; hence its lower and upper endpoints are valid bounds for every point in $B$. If $B_k$ is a nested sequence of boxes with diameters tending to zero, their limit point is $x$, and the precisions $p_k$ tend to infinity in one fixed exponent range large enough to avoid overflow, then the interval endpoints tend to $f(x)$. Under the Lipschitz hypothesis in [[alg-lipschitz-midpoint-box-lower-bound]], its lower bounds are valid on $B$ and tend to $f(x)$ on every such shrinking sequence.

For each $k \in \mathbb{N}$ let $I_k = [a_k, b_k]$ be a closed bounded interval
with $a_k \le b_k$ ([[def-interval]]), and suppose the family is **nested**:

$$I_{k+1} \subseteq I_k \qquad (k \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Write $\ell_k = b_k - a_k \ge 0$ for the length of $I_k$. Then:

1. $\displaystyle\bigcap_{k \in \mathbb{N}} I_k$ is **nonempty**. More precisely,
   with $a = \sup\{a_k : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$ and
   $b = \inf\{b_k : k \in \mathbb{N}\}$, both of which exist, one has $a \le b$
   and $$\bigcap_{k \in \mathbb{N}} I_k = [a, b].$$
2. $\displaystyle\bigcap_{k \in \mathbb{N}} I_k$ is a **single point** if and only
   if $\ell_k \to 0$ ([[def-real-limit]]).

Every hypothesis is load bearing. Dropping closedness makes the intersection
empty; dropping boundedness does the same; and dropping nonemptiness of the
individual intervals is vacuously fatal.

derivations.claim: Define $h(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}g_i(x)$. This maximum exists and is one of the $m$ values by [F3]. For any $x,y\in D_0$, $|h(x)-h(y)|\le\max_i|g_i(x)-g_i(y)|$; the right-hand side tends to zero as $y\to x$ because there are finitely many continuous $g_i$. Thus $h$ is continuous.

The box $D_0$ is nonempty and compact by [F1]. Hence $h[D_0]$ is nonempty and compact by [F2], and therefore closed and bounded. By the boundedness definition and [F6], there are $c\in\mathbb R$ and $r>0$ such that $h[D_0]\subseteq(c-r,c+r)$, so $c-r$ is a lower bound. Let $\delta_*=\inf h[D_0]$, which exists by [F4]. For every $\eta>0$, [F4] gives $y\in h[D_0]$ with $\delta_*\le y<\delta_*+\eta$; by [F6] every open ball around $\delta_*$ meets $h[D_0]$. Thus $\delta_*\in\overline{h[D_0]}$ by [F5], and closedness gives $\delta_*\in h[D_0]$. So $h$ attains its minimum $\delta_*$ on $D_0$.

Suppose the unlimited procedure split infinitely many boxes. The split tree is binary and finitely branching, so it has an infinite nested branch: at each node choose its first child with infinitely many split descendants, if one exists, and otherwise its second child. This rule is deterministic. Along this branch, longest-side bisection makes every coordinate width tend to zero: for any $\eta>0$, each coordinate can be halved while its width is at least $\eta$ only finitely many times, and each split of a box with maximum width at least $\eta$ halves one such longest coordinate. Hence all coordinate widths, and the box diameters, tend to zero. The nested interval property gives a unique point $x$ in the intersection of the branch boxes.

If $C=\emptyset$, then every $x\in D_0$ has some $g_i(x)>0$, so $h(x)>0$. Since $h$ attains its minimum, $\delta_*=h(x_*)>0$ at a minimizing point $x_*$. This is the required uniform margin and proves the converse.

By the margin hypothesis and [F3], choose an index $i$ with $g_i(x)=h(x)\ge\delta$. The interval soundness and consistency result [F8], under the valid-DAG and precision hypotheses [A1], gives $\ell_i(B_k)\to g_i(x)$ along the branch. Thus for some finite $k$ the lower bound is positive. The procedure would then certify $B_k$ empty and would not generate its branch child, contradicting the infinite branch.

The finite split tree has finitely many generated leaves. Every unpruned positive-width leaf is split by [F7], so any remaining unpruned leaf is a singleton. At such a point $x$, the margin gives some $g_i(x)\ge\delta$ by [F3]; repeated singleton queries use strictly increasing precision by the schedule in [[alg-certified-constraint-emptiness-search]]. Their lower bounds converge to this value by [A1] and [F8], so after finitely many singleton queries one is positive. Every leaf is therefore certified empty after finitely many finite-time oracle calls. The queue empties, and the certified-empty leaf cover of $D_0$ proves infeasibility.

Let $K$ be the finite total number of oracle calls established in step 3.1. A budget of at least $K$ does not exhaust before the queue empties, so [[alg-certified-constraint-emptiness-search]] returns the same infeasibility certificate; a smaller budget may return only its explicit budget-exhausted status.

Input a finite-dimensional compact continuous box $X=\prod_{j=1}^n[\alpha_j,\beta_j]$ with $n\ge0$ and finite ordered endpoints, a finite integer box
$$Z=\prod_{j=1}^r\bigl([a_j,b_j]\cap\mathbb Z\bigr),\qquad r\ge0,\quad a_j,b_j\in\mathbb Z,\quad a_j\le b_j,$$
a continuous objective and its inequality constraints on $X\times Z$ represented by finite factorable expression DAGs, tolerance $\varepsilon>0$, positive integer node budget $N$, a verified interval/relaxation rule table, precision $p\ge2$, a dyadic interval format with fixed exponent bounds, and deterministic verified bound oracles. Every relaxation rule must meet [[alg-factorable-mccormick-box-relaxation]], and every bound used for pruning or a gap certificate must satisfy [[thm-factorable-dual-certificate-is-valid-box-lower-bound]] on each nonempty feasible node. The integer set $Z$ is finite by boundedness of every coordinate interval. Every main-tree node evaluation consumes one unit of the budget and each oracle call returns in finite time or gives an explicit unavailable status.

When $r=0$, the empty product defining $Z$ is the singleton assignment with no integer coordinates. When $n=0$, $X$ is the singleton empty tuple. Before any oracle or supplier call, represent it instead by a dummy continuous coordinate in $[0,0]$ and make every objective and constraint DAG ignore that coordinate. Run all instructions below on this one-dimensional box; on return, delete the dummy coordinate from every witness and ledger box. This bijective representation preserves all objective and constraint values and admits every spatial subcall without excluding purely integer inputs.

A main-tree node is $(J,B)$, where $J$ is a product of bounded integer intervals and $B\subseteq X$ is a continuous box. Relax each integer interval to its real hull and call [[alg-factorable-mccormick-box-relaxation]] on the objective DAG and all constraint DAGs over $B$ times those hulls, passing the declared precision and interval format. A verified dual lower bound is valid on the original integer-feasible node by [[thm-factorable-dual-certificate-is-valid-box-lower-bound]]. The oracle may also return a feasible mixed-integer witness with a verified objective upper bound, a proof of emptiness, or an unavailable status. The latter never supplies a finite lower bound. Store lower bounds for terminal nodes. Retain certified-empty nodes and their proofs in the terminal ledger, excluding them from lower-bound comparisons, closure tests, and split selection; they require no lower bound. Close a node not certified empty only when its lower bound is at least $U-\varepsilon$, retaining that bound in the global ledger.

Initialize the terminal ledger with the root $(Z,X)$, a FIFO queue containing that unevaluated root, remaining budget $N$, incumbent $U=+\infty$, and no incumbent witness. Each returned feasible witness with verified upper bound $U_x<U$ replaces the incumbent and sets $U=U_x$; retain the earlier witness on an equal bound. Keep unevaluated nodes in the FIFO queue ordered by creation. Generate lower integer children before upper integer children, and lower-half continuous children before upper-half children, appending children in this order. Before each node evaluation, if no call remains, return the current ledger with `budget-exhausted`; otherwise evaluate the oldest pending node and charge one call. When no node is pending, return infeasible if every terminal node is certified empty. If every terminal node not certified empty has a valid lower bound, let $L$ be the least such bound; when $U$ is finite and $U-L\le\varepsilon$, return the feasible witness and global epsilon certificate. Retain bounds for closed nodes in this calculation. Otherwise choose an evaluated nonclosed node not certified empty with least lower bound, breaking ties by creation order. If an integer interval has at least two values, choose the least-index such coordinate and split at $m=\lfloor(a+b)/2\rfloor$ into the disjoint children $[a,m]\cap\mathbb Z$ and $[m+1,b]\cap\mathbb Z$. Otherwise, if a continuous width is positive, split a longest continuous side at its exact midpoint, using least coordinate index ties. Children replace the parent in the coverage frontier and are evaluated before another split. A mixed singleton node that is neither certified empty nor closed by the gap test returns `inconclusive`.

If a mixed relaxation bound is unavailable or non-finite on a node not certified empty, stop the main tree and, if at least one call remains for each assignment, enumerate every $z\in Z$ in lexicographic order. Substitute $z$ into the objective and constraint DAGs to form $f_z$ and $C_z=\{x\in X:g_i(x,z)\le0\text{ for all }i\}$, then invoke [[alg-certified-spatial-branch-and-bound]] on $(X,C_z,f_z)$ with the continuous budget allocated to that assignment. Explicitly, with $M=|Z|$ and remaining integer budget $R\ge M$, set $q=\lfloor R/M\rfloor$ and $h=R-Mq$. Give the first $h$ assignments $q+1$ calls each and the remaining $M-h$ assignments $q$ calls each. These are positive integer budgets summing to $R$. If any assignment has an oracle failure, a pending or missing report, or a terminal leaf not certified empty without a valid finite lower bound, return inconclusive. If every assignment is certified infeasible, return infeasible before taking any minimum. Otherwise the complete assignment ledgers have a nonempty finite collection of terminal leaves not certified empty. Let $L$ be the minimum of their lower bounds. Let $U$ be the minimum of the feasible upper bounds returned by these ledgers if there are any, and set $U=+\infty$ if there is no feasible witness. Return a global epsilon certificate only when $U$ is finite and $U-L\le\varepsilon$; otherwise return inconclusive. If enumeration does not fit in the remaining budget, return inconclusive. This fallback is finite because $Z$ is finite. The method makes no polynomial-complexity claim.

For every admissible finite oracle call and every positive integer budget $N$, [[alg-certified-spatial-branch-and-bound]] terminates after at most $N$ calls and returns exactly one of: a verified epsilon-global certificate, a certified infeasibility result, or an inconclusive budget/oracle status.

derivations.claim: The main tree can make at most $N$ calls because each call decreases the remaining integer budget. Every integer interval split has at least two values and produces finite children; every continuous split produces two children. Thus no one iteration creates an infinite operation sequence.

Write $M=|Z|\ge1$ and let $R\le N$ be the remaining integer budget after main-tree calls. The fallback is entered only if $R\ge M$. Input a finite-dimensional compact continuous box $X=\prod_{j=1}^n[\alpha_j,\beta_j]$ with $n\ge0$ and finite ordered endpoints, a finite integer box
$$Z=\prod_{j=1}^r\bigl([a_j,b_j]\cap\mathbb Z\bigr),\qquad r\ge0,\quad a_j,b_j\in\mathbb Z,\quad a_j\le b_j,$$
a continuous objective and its inequality constraints on $X\times Z$ represented by finite factorable expression DAGs, tolerance $\varepsilon>0$, positive integer node budget $N$, a verified interval/relaxation rule table, precision $p\ge2$, a dyadic interval format with fixed exponent bounds, and deterministic verified bound oracles. Every relaxation rule must meet [[alg-factorable-mccormick-box-relaxation]], and every bound used for pruning or a gap certificate must satisfy [[thm-factorable-dual-certificate-is-valid-box-lower-bound]] on each nonempty feasible node. The integer set $Z$ is finite by boundedness of every coordinate interval. Every main-tree node evaluation consumes one unit of the budget and each oracle call returns in finite time or gives an explicit unavailable status.

When $r=0$, the empty product defining $Z$ is the singleton assignment with no integer coordinates. When $n=0$, $X$ is the singleton empty tuple. Before any oracle or supplier call, represent it instead by a dummy continuous coordinate in $[0,0]$ and make every objective and constraint DAG ignore that coordinate. Run all instructions below on this one-dimensional box; on return, delete the dummy coordinate from every witness and ledger box. This bijective representation preserves all objective and constraint values and admits every spatial subcall without excluding purely integer inputs.

A main-tree node is $(J,B)$, where $J$ is a product of bounded integer intervals and $B\subseteq X$ is a continuous box. Relax each integer interval to its real hull and call [[alg-factorable-mccormick-box-relaxation]] on the objective DAG and all constraint DAGs over $B$ times those hulls, passing the declared precision and interval format. A verified dual lower bound is valid on the original integer-feasible node by [[thm-factorable-dual-certificate-is-valid-box-lower-bound]]. The oracle may also return a feasible mixed-integer witness with a verified objective upper bound, a proof of emptiness, or an unavailable status. The latter never supplies a finite lower bound. Store lower bounds for terminal nodes. Retain certified-empty nodes and their proofs in the terminal ledger, excluding them from lower-bound comparisons, closure tests, and split selection; they require no lower bound. Close a node not certified empty only when its lower bound is at least $U-\varepsilon$, retaining that bound in the global ledger.

Initialize the terminal ledger with the root $(Z,X)$, a FIFO queue containing that unevaluated root, remaining budget $N$, incumbent $U=+\infty$, and no incumbent witness. Each returned feasible witness with verified upper bound $U_x<U$ replaces the incumbent and sets $U=U_x$; retain the earlier witness on an equal bound. Keep unevaluated nodes in the FIFO queue ordered by creation. Generate lower integer children before upper integer children, and lower-half continuous children before upper-half children, appending children in this order. Before each node evaluation, if no call remains, return the current ledger with `budget-exhausted`; otherwise evaluate the oldest pending node and charge one call. When no node is pending, return infeasible if every terminal node is certified empty. If every terminal node not certified empty has a valid lower bound, let $L$ be the least such bound; when $U$ is finite and $U-L\le\varepsilon$, return the feasible witness and global epsilon certificate. Retain bounds for closed nodes in this calculation. Otherwise choose an evaluated nonclosed node not certified empty with least lower bound, breaking ties by creation order. If an integer interval has at least two values, choose the least-index such coordinate and split at $m=\lfloor(a+b)/2\rfloor$ into the disjoint children $[a,m]\cap\mathbb Z$ and $[m+1,b]\cap\mathbb Z$. Otherwise, if a continuous width is positive, split a longest continuous side at its exact midpoint, using least coordinate index ties. Children replace the parent in the coverage frontier and are evaluated before another split. A mixed singleton node that is neither certified empty nor closed by the gap test returns `inconclusive`.

If a mixed relaxation bound is unavailable or non-finite on a node not certified empty, stop the main tree and, if at least one call remains for each assignment, enumerate every $z\in Z$ in lexicographic order. Substitute $z$ into the objective and constraint DAGs to form $f_z$ and $C_z=\{x\in X:g_i(x,z)\le0\text{ for all }i\}$, then invoke [[alg-certified-spatial-branch-and-bound]] on $(X,C_z,f_z)$ with the continuous budget allocated to that assignment. Explicitly, with $M=|Z|$ and remaining integer budget $R\ge M$, set $q=\lfloor R/M\rfloor$ and $h=R-Mq$. Give the first $h$ assignments $q+1$ calls each and the remaining $M-h$ assignments $q$ calls each. These are positive integer budgets summing to $R$. If any assignment has an oracle failure, a pending or missing report, or a terminal leaf not certified empty without a valid finite lower bound, return inconclusive. If every assignment is certified infeasible, return infeasible before taking any minimum. Otherwise the complete assignment ledgers have a nonempty finite collection of terminal leaves not certified empty. Let $L$ be the minimum of their lower bounds. Let $U$ be the minimum of the feasible upper bounds returned by these ledgers if there are any, and set $U=+\infty$ if there is no feasible witness. Return a global epsilon certificate only when $U$ is finite and $U-L\le\varepsilon$; otherwise return inconclusive. If enumeration does not fit in the remaining budget, return inconclusive. This fallback is finite because $Z$ is finite. The method makes no polynomial-complexity claim.

Suppose [[alg-factorable-mccormick-box-relaxation]] returns a certified convex relaxation $(R_B,\phi_B)$ of an original problem on a box $B$ with $B\cap C
e\emptyset$, and a dual-feasible pair $(\lambda,
u)$ with a verified lower bound $\ell\le q(\lambda,
u)$. Then $\ell$ is a valid lower bound for the original box problem:
$$\ell\le \inf_{x\in B\cap C} f(x).$$
This certificate applies only to the stated relaxation and its verified coefficient/domain enclosures. A solver residual or an approximate dual objective without a verified lower bound is not a certificate.

Input a compact-box instance $(D_0,C,f)$ from [[def-spatial-global-optimization-problem]], a tolerance $\varepsilon>0$, a positive integer node budget $N$, and a deterministic box-report oracle implementing [[def-spatial-box-bound-certificate]]. Every oracle call must finish in finite time or return an unavailable status. The budget counts each oracle call, including the root and both children after every split. The oracle may request higher precision on a repeated box; each such refinement is another counted call.

Initialize a leaf ledger with the root box $D_0$, no incumbent ($U=+\infty$), and zero calls. Evaluate the root first. Before every oracle call, if the call counter is already $N$, return the complete current ledger with budget-exhausted; otherwise call the oracle and increment the counter by one. Store every returned field. A feasible witness $(x,U_x)$ updates the incumbent upper bound to $U=\min U_x$. An empty-box proof marks that leaf empty; retain the leaf and its proof in the ledger, but exclude it from lower-bound comparisons, closure tests, and split candidates. For constraints $g_i(x)\le0$, a sound interval lower bound $\underline g_i(B)>0$ is an empty-box proof. Store every valid lower bound $\ell_B$ even if the leaf is later closed. Every evaluated leaf not certified empty requires a finite lower bound; if that field is missing, non-finite, or unavailable, return inconclusive. A certified-empty leaf requires no lower bound.

Whenever all current leaves have been evaluated, first return infeasible if they are all certified empty. Otherwise put $L=\min\{\ell_B:B\text{ is not certified empty}\}$. If $U<+\infty$, $L$ is finite, and $U-L\le\varepsilon$, return a feasible witness and the epsilon-global certificate $(L,U)$. Mark any leaf not certified empty with $\ell_B\ge U-\varepsilon$ closed while retaining its lower bound.

If no certificate is returned and no pending child awaits evaluation, split the nonclosed leaf not certified empty with least lower bound; ties use creation order. In a box with positive widths, bisect a longest coordinate at its exact midpoint, using the least coordinate index among ties. Replace the parent by its two closed subboxes, which cover it. Create and evaluate the child with the lower half of the split coordinate first, then the upper-half child. Pending children are evaluated in that order before the next all-leaves check or split. In the unconstrained mode, the oracle returns the exact midpoint as a feasible witness and exact objective value; the termination theorem uses this mode. For a zero-width singleton that has not been certified, request a deterministic higher-precision report for that same point; each refinement consumes one call. If refinement is unavailable, return inconclusive. When no certificate or infeasibility result has been established and another oracle call is needed after $N$ calls, the pre-call guard returns the complete current ledger with no optimality claim. This finite-budget procedure is global-search bookkeeping: a local stationary point or a solver tolerance is not a lower-bound certificate.

Fix an instance $(D_0,C,f)$ from [[def-spatial-global-optimization-problem]] and a closed subbox $B\subseteq D_0$. A **certified box report** may contain any combination of the following fields:

- A **feasible witness** $(x_B,U_B)$, with $x_B\in B\cap C$ and a verified upper bound $f(x_B)\le U_B$.
- A **lower bound** $\ell_B\in\mathbb R$ satisfying $\ell_B\le f(x)$ for every $x\in B\cap C$. This pointwise condition is vacuous when $B\cap C=\emptyset$; when $B\cap C\ne\emptyset$, it is equivalent to $\ell_B\le\inf_{x\in B\cap C}f(x)$.
- An **empty-box proof** establishing $B\cap C=\emptyset$.
- A non-finite or unavailable status, which makes no feasibility, lower-bound, or optimality claim.

A box is **closed** for a requested tolerance $\varepsilon>0$ only when it has a lower bound and $\ell_B\ge U-\varepsilon$, where $U$ is the best currently verified feasible upper bound. Closing a box stops further subdivision but retains its lower bound in the global ledger. A report lacking a required field is not repaired by a numerical guess.

derivations.claim: The root node contains every feasible pair in $X\times Z$; the dummy-singleton representation, when used, is bijective and preserves objective and constraint values. Each integer branch preserves the union of the allowed integer values by [F1], and each continuous branch covers its parent box by [F1]. Removing a node only with an emptiness proof cannot remove a feasible pair. Induction on the finite number of expansions shows every feasible pair lies in a nonempty terminal node, or in one of the fixed-$z$ continuous ledgers of the fallback.

For any feasible pair $(x,z)$ choose its terminal node or fallback leaf as in step 1.1. For a main-tree node, the point $(x,z)$ makes the real-hull feasible set nonempty, and the algorithm accepts a relaxation bound only with the certified relaxation, dual feasibility, and verified dual-value lower bound required by [F2]; hence its lower bound is at most $f(x,z)$. For a fixed-$z$ continuous leaf the same pointwise inequality follows from [F4]. Since $L$ is the least bound over the complete global ledger, $L\le f(x,z)$ for every feasible pair, hence $L\le f^*$.

The feasible incumbent satisfies $f(\hat x,\hat z)\le U$. The certificate condition then gives $f(\hat x,\hat z)\le U\le L+\varepsilon\le f^*+\varepsilon$, proving the global gap claim. If every terminal node is certified empty, step 1.1 shows no feasible pair exists.

Assume AC and let $f=(f_t)_{t\in T}$ be a real Gaussian process with mean
$m$ and covariance kernel $k$; when $m$ and $k$ are specified as a prior,
the canonical cylinder-space process exists by
[[thm-gaussian-process-exists-from-mean-and-positive-semidefinite-covariance-kernel]].
Let $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in T^n$ and $X_*=(x_1^*,\ldots,x_p^*)\in T^p$,
where $n,p\ge1$ and repeated indices are allowed. Write
$f_X=(f_{x_i})_{i=1}^n$, $f_{X_*}=(f_{x_j^*})_{j=1}^p$,
$m_X=(m(x_i))_{i=1}^n$, and $m_*=(m(x_j^*))_{j=1}^p$. For finite lists
$A=(a_i)$ and $B=(b_j)$, define
$K_{AB}=(k(a_i,b_j))_{i,j}$.

Let $\epsilon\sim N_n(0,R)$ be independent of the process, where $R$ is
symmetric positive semidefinite, and set $Y=f_X+\epsilon$. Assume the
observed covariance $C=K_{XX}+R$ is positive definite. Then a version of the
conditional law of $f_{X_*}$ given $Y=y$ is, for every $y\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$N_p\!\left(m_*+K_{*X}C^{-1}(y-m_X),\;K_{**}-K_{*X}C^{-1}K_{X*}\right).$$
The displayed conditional covariance is positive semidefinite and may be
singular; $K_{XX}$ and $K_{**}$ may also be singular. If a prediction-noise
vector $\eta_*\sim N_p(0,R_*)$ jointly independent of the process and
$\epsilon$ is added to $f_{X_*}$, with $R_*$ symmetric positive semidefinite,
the conditional mean is unchanged and
$R_*$ is added to the conditional covariance. The displayed kernel is a
version defined at every $y$; conditional-law versions are determined only
$P_Y$-almost surely.

For computation, the occurrences of $C^{-1}v$ mean solving $Cu=v$. Since
$C$ is positive definite, its Cholesky factorization and forward/back
substitution evaluate these solves without forming $C^{-1}$.

Input a candidate list $X=(c_1,\ldots,c_M)$, a horizon $N$, an initial-list length $s$, a real-mean candidate $m$, a kernel candidate $k$, an observation-variance candidate $\sigma^2$, coefficients $(b_t)_{0\le t<N}$, an initial data list $(x_i,y_i)_{i=1}^s$, an observation oracle $O$, and a selector that is either the exact rule below or a certified approximate rule below. For $N=0$, the coefficient list is empty. First validate that $X$ is nonempty, finite, and ordered; $N$ and $s$ are integers with $N\ge0$ and $0\le s\le N$; every initial site lies in $X$; all mean, kernel, noise, coefficient, and initial-observation values are finite reals; the kernel matrix on $X$ is symmetric positive semidefinite; $\sigma^2\ge0$; and each required $b_t$ is defined and nonnegative. If any validation fails, return `inadmissible-model` before computing a posterior. The observation oracle must finish each call in finite time and return either a finite real observation or `observation-unavailable`. For a true-posterior interpretation, the initial sites are fixed before their observations and each observation is $f(x_i)+\xi_i$ under this model, with errors independent centered Gaussian variables of variance $\sigma^2$ and independent of the entire process. In this interpretation, whether a call returns a value or `observation-unavailable` must be a deterministic measurable function of the already observed history and selected site, decided without inspecting the unobserved process or the fresh noise; thus availability conveys no additional information. Otherwise the procedure computes only the all-data-vector posterior kernel for the specified surrogate and makes no claim that it is the conditional law of an externally supplied data-generating process. The Axiom of Choice is included as required by [[thm-finite-gaussian-process-posterior-and-predictive-laws]].

Denote the sites in the accumulated observation trace, in observation order, by $x_1,\ldots,x_t$; these are not the candidate-list indices and may repeat. Write $X_t=(x_1,\ldots,x_t)$, $y=(y_1,\ldots,y_t)$, $m_{X_t}=(m(x_i))_{i\le t}$, and $k_t(x)=(k(x_i,x))_{i\le t}$. Initialize the trace with the given data and let its length be $t=s$. If $t=0$, the current state is the prior with $\mu_0(x)=m(x)$ and $v_0(x)=k(x,x)$, without a matrix solve. If $t\ge1$, form $K_t=(k(x_i,x_j))_{i,j\le t}$ and $C_t=K_t+\sigma^2 I$. If $C_t$ is not certified positive definite, or its Cholesky factorization or required solves are unavailable, return `posterior-solve-unavailable` with the initial trace and no posterior state. Otherwise compute the current posterior by the formulas below. At every later history length $t\ge1$, use the same rule to compute its state immediately after the new observation is appended. Never use a pseudoinverse or clip a negative variance. In particular, this state update is performed after the final observation at history length $N$, before a `complete` return.

If the initialized history already has length $t=N$, return `complete` with the initial trace, its computed posterior state, and the empty list of acquisition errors. Otherwise $t<N$, and for each candidate compute
$$\mu_t(x)=m(x)+k_t(x)^T C_t^{-1}(y-m_{X_t})$$
$$v_t(x)=k(x,x)-k_t(x)^T C_t^{-1}k_t(x),\qquad s_t(x)=\sqrt{v_t(x)}$$
where the observed covariance and solves satisfy the hypotheses of [[thm-finite-gaussian-process-posterior-and-predictive-laws]]. At $t=0$, use the prior formulas above. At $t\ge1$, its conditional covariance is positive semidefinite, so $v_t(x)\ge0$; [[thm-of-square-roots]] supplies the unique nonnegative square root used here. If nonnegativity of a computed $v_t(x)$ cannot be verified, return `posterior-solve-unavailable` with the current trace and last valid state. Form $a_t(x)=\mu_t(x)+b_t s_t(x)$ and inspect all $M$ candidates. The exact selector returns the least-index maximizer with $\delta_t=0$. A certified approximate selector must be a deterministic measurable function of the finite observation history and return a candidate $c_{j_t}$ with verified $\delta_t\ge0$ satisfying $a_t(c_{j_t})\ge\max_{x\in X}a_t(x)-\delta_t$. If no such comparison certificate is available, return `acquisition-inconclusive` with the current trace and state. Record every $\delta_t$.

Call $O$ at the selected candidate. If it returns `observation-unavailable`, return that status with the current trace and state, without appending a value. If it returns a finite real, append the pair $(x_{t+1},y_{t+1})=(c_{j_t},O(c_{j_t}))$, using the value from this single call, increment $t$ by one, and compute the new posterior state by the rule above; if this solve is unavailable, return `posterior-solve-unavailable` with the updated trace and last valid state. If $t=N$, return `complete` with the full trace, posterior state at history length $N$, and recorded acquisition errors. Otherwise continue to the next acquisition stage. For a deterministic simulator or a misspecified prior, these formulas describe only the chosen surrogate model; the algorithm asserts no generic regret, global-optimality, or model-truth result.
